qs.q: A patient presents with deep tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after falling on an outstretched hand. Which underlying carpal bone is most likely clinically suspected of being fractured?
qs.e: The floor of the anatomical snuffbox is primarily formed by the scaphoid bone, which is vulnerable during falls.
qs.s: Weekly Year 1: Anatomy Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: When examining the carpal bones during an osteology practical, a student identifies the pisiform. Which muscular tendon attaches directly to this bone?
qs.e: The flexor carpi ulnaris tendon attaches to the pisiform bone, which also gives origin to the abductor digiti minimi. Flexor carpi radialis does not attach to this pisiform landmark.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: In a carpal bone osteology practical, a student labels several bones including the pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, and hamate. Which of the remaining carpal bones completes the full set of eight?
qs.e: The full set of carpal bones includes the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform, trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate. Calcaneus, talus, and cuboid are tarsal bones of the foot.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: A student palpates a small carpal bone on the ulnar side of the proximal wrist row. Which muscular tendon directly attaches to this specific bone, the pisiform?
qs.e: The flexor carpi ulnaris tendon attaches to the pisiform bone, which also gives origin to the abductor digiti minimi. The other tendons insert or originate elsewhere in the wrist and hand.
qs.s: PAT III — Progress Assessment Test (8 November 2019) — Revision Guide: MCQs

qs.q: Which carpal bone is directly identified as bone X in the distal carpal row?
qs.e: The trapezium is identified as bone X in the distal carpal row. The scaphoid and lunate belong to the proximal row.
qs.s: Limb Anatomy Revision — Lower & Upper Limb: MCQs

qs.q: In identifying the carpal bones during an anatomy practical, a student locates the pisiform bone. Within the tendon of which muscle does this sesamoid bone develop?
qs.e: The pisiform bone is a sesamoid bone located directly within the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris. Flexor carpi radialis inserts on the base of the second and third metacarpals instead.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: While tracing the carpal bones from proximal to distal and lateral to medial during an osteology practical, a student identifies the triquetrum. Which structure is correctly paired with its sequence in this mnemonic?
qs.e: In the standard anatomical mapping, structure 3 is the triquetrum, structure 4 is the trapezium, structure 5 is the trapezoid, and structure 7 is the hamate. The wrong options misattribute these specific numbered identifications.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

qs.q: While studying the carpal bones, a medical student focuses on the pisiform. Which of the following statements regarding its muscular attachments is correct?
o: Flexor carpi ulnaris inserts into it, and abductor digiti minimi originates from it
Extensor carpi ulnaris inserts into it, and flexor digitorum profundus originates from it
Palmaris longus inserts into it, and adductor pollicis originates from it
Flexor carpi radialis inserts into it, and abductor pollicis brevis originates from it
qs.e: The pisiform bone acts as a sesamoid bone within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, which inserts into it, while abductor digiti minimi originates from it. Flexor carpi radialis inserts on the base of the second and third metacarpals.
qs.s: SDL Revision Mock Marathon — Upper Limb, Histology & Embryology —: MCQs

ai.title: Carpal Bones
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The carpal bones form the wrist’s complex joint, allowing flexion, extension, radial‑ulnar deviation and grip. Understanding their anatomy aids diagnosis of fractures, ligament injuries and tropical infections that affect the hand.

sections.p: The wrist contains eight carpal bones arranged in two rows. They articulate with the radius, ulna and metacarpals, forming a hinge‑like joint that balances stability and mobility.

The proximal row lies anterior to the distal row. Each bone has a specific shape: the scaphoid is boat‑shaped, the lunate is crescentic, the triquetrum is triangular, the capitate is largest, and the pisiform is a small sesamoid.

The scaphoid articulates with the radius and trapezium; the lunate with the radius and triquetrum; the triquetrum with the lunate and capitate; the capitate with the lunate and hamate; the pisiform lies over the flexor carpi ulnaris.
The scaphoid receives blood from the radial artery via the dorsal and palmar branches; its distal pole is most vulnerable to avascular necrosis.
Sensory innervation is by the superficial radial, median and ulnar nerves; motor supply to intrinsic hand muscles is via the median and ulnar nerves.
Provide a stable hinge for wrist flexion/extension and a pivot for radial‑ulnar deviation. They also transmit forces from the hand to the forearm.
Fractures are common, especially of the scaphoid. In low‑resource settings, infections such as osteomyelitis from malaria or TB can involve carpal bones.
b: Scaphoid fracture: wrist pain, positive Watson‑Jones test, risk of AVN

t.b: Shows fracture lines; absence of fracture may miss occult scaphoid fracture
Detects occult fractures and early osteomyelitis; may be unavailable
Can identify soft‑tissue abscesses around carpal bones when MRI is not available

sections.p: Ask for pain on radial deviation (scaphoid), ulnar deviation (lunate), and check for tenderness over the pisiform. In tropical patients, consider septic arthritis of the wrist.
Severe wrist pain with swelling, inability to move the wrist, or signs of systemic infection.

faq.q: What is the most common carpal fracture?
faq.a: The scaphoid, due to its position and blood supply.

faq.q: How do you differentiate a scaphoid from a lunate fracture clinically?
faq.a: Scaphoid pain is elicited by radial deviation (Watson‑Jones); lunate pain is more with ulnar deviation.

faq.q: Why is AVN a concern after a scaphoid fracture?
faq.a: The distal pole’s blood supply is tenuous; fracture can disrupt it, leading to bone death.

exam: 1. A 25‑year‑old man falls on an outstretched hand, reports wrist pain. Which test best detects a scaphoid fracture? — Watson‑Jones test; positive if pain on radial deviation with wrist flexion.

2. A patient with chronic malaria presents with wrist swelling and pain. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis of the wrist; look for fever, elevated CRP, and consider MRI if available.
3. Which carpal bone is most at risk for avascular necrosis after fracture? — Scaphoid; explain its blood supply and why the distal pole is vulnerable.
4. A child has a tender, swollen wrist after a fall. X‑ray is normal. What next? — Obtain an MRI or CT to rule out occult scaphoid fracture; if unavailable, repeat X‑ray in 10–14 days.
5. Why is the pisiform considered a sesamoid bone? — It lies within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, reducing friction and acting as a pulley.
6. A patient with HIV presents with wrist pain and a history of intravenous drug use. What complication should you consider? — Osteomyelitis; obtain blood cultures and consider MRI.
7. What is the clinical significance of the lunate bone’s position? — It forms the central pivot for wrist motion and is involved in the perilunate dislocation mechanism.
8. In a low‑resource setting, which simple bedside test can suggest a scaphoid fracture when imaging is unavailable? — The Watson‑Jones test; if positive, immobilise and refer for imaging.
